"""

How it works

The plugin makes a land cover map from a drone image or an aerial photo. It does not look at single pixels. First it cuts the image into objects (pieces of a field, a roof, a tree crown), and then it learns from you what is what.

Why objects and not pixels? A single pixel tells you only its colour. An object also has texture, shape, height and surroundings, and the map does not come out littered with single specks.

What you need

  • An RGB image: a drone orthomosaic, an aerial photo or a satellite scene. Three bands are enough: red, green and blue.
  • An elevation model (DSM): optional, but very helpful. Without it the plugin measures 19 features, with it 24, including height above ground. That is what tells a roof from asphalt and a tree from a lawn.

Ordinary drone cameras do not record near infrared, so there is no NDVI here. It is replaced by visible-band indices (ExG greenness, VARI, NGRDI), texture, shape and height.

Step 1: segmentation

The most important field is Object size. There is one rule: an object must be smaller than the narrowest thing you want to show on the map. For fields and roofs 5-20 m² works well; for single trees 2-5 m².

After segmentation, look at the result on the map and check two things: that no object lies on two different kinds of land at once (that is a problem, so make the objects smaller), and that a uniform meadow has not broken into hundreds of specks (that is only an inconvenience).

On a large image, first tick "Process only what is visible on screen" and choose the object size on a small part.

Step 2: classes and examples

Add the classes you want to distinguish, then click the objects on the map that belong to them. Three things decide the result:

  • Spread examples over the whole image. Light and shadow change from place to place.
  • Show every variant of a class. "Bare soil" is freshly ploughed land, a trodden path and a dry embankment.
  • Pick only what you recognise without hesitation. One wrong example teaches the plugin a wrong rule. Leave out objects that lie on the border of two classes.

10-20 examples per class are enough to start. You will add more anyway.

Step 3: training and map

Before you start, click "Can the classes be told apart?". If a pair scores poorly, there is no point in more work: either add examples or merge those classes.

Correcting the map is not a failure, it is the method. The first map is never good. Look over all of it, write down the kinds of errors, add a few examples of each kind in different places and repeat. Two or three rounds bring the most.

Greenness refinement helps when you map fields: a strip of grass between plots is often narrower than an object and gets lost. This option hands the decision to single pixels, but only for the two selected classes. Note: recovered strips come out slightly wider than in reality, so be careful when reporting their area.

Step 4: how good is this map

Here the plugin does something QGIS lacks: it computes accuracy the way reviewers and good practice require.

  1. It draws check points, never on objects used for training.
  2. You label each point by looking at the image alone. Turn off the classification map layer before you start; otherwise the plugin's answer influences your judgement and the result is inflated.
  3. You get the error matrix, user's and producer's accuracy for each class, and overall accuracy.

With stratified sampling, small classes get proportionally many points, so the share of points is not the share of area. That is why the plugin also reports area-weighted figures and estimated class areas with confidence intervals. Cite those in a publication.

What stays in the project

  • GeoAI objects: a polygon layer; its attribute table holds all measured features of each object, the column train_class (your examples) and map_class (the result).
  • GeoAI check points: points with the label from the image, the class from the map and the sampling stratum.
  • A saved GeoTIFF with a .qml style file next to it.

Faster and more accurate

__INSTALL__

Where the method comes from

SLIC segmentation (Achanta et al., 2012), GLCM texture (Haralick et al., 1973), ExG greenness (Woebbecke et al., 1995), Random Forest (Breiman, 2001; Belgiu and Drăguţ, 2016), class separability with the Jeffries-Matusita distance, and accuracy assessment following Congalton and Green, Olofsson et al. (2014) and Stehman (2014).
